questions.q: Match each investment to what it makes you.
pairs: A lender to a company or government
One of many investors pooling money
A lender to the UK government
questions.why: Shares are ownership, bonds are loans (gilts are UK government bonds), funds pool money to buy many investments.

questions.q: A share costs {p} and pays a dividend of {d} a year. What's its dividend yield, in %?
A bond pays a coupon of {c} a year on £100 face value. You buy it for {p}. What's its current yield, in %?
questions.why: Current yield = coupon ÷ price paid: {c} ÷ {p} = {answer}%. Pay less, get a higher yield.

questions.q: A company goes bust. Who is usually paid back last?
questions.why: Owners come last, after lenders and suppliers, and usually get nothing. That's part of why shares are riskier than bonds.

questions.q: Once a company pays a dividend, it has to keep paying it every year.
questions.why: Dividends aren't guaranteed. Companies can cut or stop them, especially in hard times.

questions.q: Put these in order from usually least risky to most risky.
items: Fund holding hundreds of companies' shares
questions.why: Protected cash can't fall; gilts are very safe lenders' claims; a spread of shares swings but rarely all fail; one small company can go to zero.

questions.q: Interest rates rise sharply. What usually happens to the price of existing bonds with low fixed coupons?
questions.why: New bonds pay more, so old low-coupon bonds are less attractive and their price falls until their yield competes.

questions.q: Money you'll need in the next year is usually better invested in shares than kept in savings.
questions.why: Shares can fall a lot in the short term. Money needed within about five years usually belongs in cash.

questions.q: What's the main advantage of a fund over buying a few individual shares?
options: It spreads your money over many investments, so one failure hurts less
It guarantees you won't lose money
questions.why: Funds give diversification in one purchase. They still charge fees and can still fall.

questions.q: Explain why shares have usually returned more than bonds over the long run.

ideas.label: Shares are riskier: owners are paid last and prices swing
Investors need a higher expected return to accept that risk

questions.model: Shares are riskier: shareholders are paid last, prices swing a lot and a company can go bust. Nobody would take that extra risk without the chance of a higher reward, so on average shares must offer a higher expected return than bonds.
questions.why: More risk has to come with more expected reward, or no one would take it.

tests.answer: Shares are riskier because owners are paid last, so investors need a higher return to make it worth it.
Because companies are bigger than governments.

questions.q: A friend says investing in shares is "just gambling". Explain one key difference.

ideas.label: Shares are part-ownership of real businesses that make profits and grow
Over the long term, investors share in that growth (gambling has a negative expected return)

questions.model: Shares are part-ownership of real businesses that make products and profits. Over the long term, investors in a broad spread of companies share in that growth, whereas in gambling the house wins on average and money just changes hands.
questions.why: Owning productive businesses has a positive expected return; most bets don't.

tests.answer: You own part of real companies that make profits, and over the long term you share in their growth.
Because you own part of a company.
